chapitres.resume: Axe 1, Représentation de soi et rapport à autrui : canons de beauté des préraphaélites aux concours de beauté, body positivity, la mode comme revendication. Grammaire : comparatifs et superlatifs, look/seem + adjectif, pronoms réfléchis et réciproques, gérondif.
chapitres.chapeau: What we show of ourselves, and how others see us, has always mattered. Painters, magazines and social networks have all set beauty norms, and people have also challenged them. Dans ce chapitre, tu lis des textes sur ces normes et tu apprends à décrire, à comparer et à donner ton avis en anglais.
objectifs: décrire l'apparence d'une personne, d'une tenue ou d'un tableau avec un vocabulaire précis ;
comparer avec les comparatifs, les superlatifs et les adverbes de degré ;
exprimer une impression avec look, seem et appear suivis d'un adjectif ;
employer les pronoms réfléchis et le réciproque each other ;
utiliser le gérondif comme sujet ou complément ;
présenter les préraphaélites, les concours de beauté, le mouvement body positivity et la mode comme revendication.

sections.titre: From the Pre-Raphaelites to beauty pageants
sections.html:
Un canon de beauté (beauty canon) est un modèle d'apparence qu'une époque considère comme idéal. Lis le texte, puis repère les traits physiques qui définissent chaque idéal.

The Pre-Raphaelite woman

In 1848, three young British painters, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, John Everett Millais and William Holman Hunt, founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in London. They wanted to paint nature in great detail and with bright colours, as artists did before the Italian painter Raphael.

Their paintings created a new ideal of female beauty: a pale complexion, long flowing hair, often red, a long neck, full lips and a dreamy, melancholy look. One of their favourite models was Elizabeth Siddal. She posed for Millais's famous painting Ophelia (1851–1852), which shows Shakespeare's heroine floating in a river. Later, Jane Morris became the face of many of Rossetti's paintings.

At the time, this look surprised many critics: these women did not fit the fashionable stereotype of the small, rosy-cheeked Victorian lady.

Beauty pageants

In the twentieth century, beauty contests, or beauty pageants, turned beauty into a public competition. The first Miss America pageant took place in Atlantic City in 1921, and Miss World was created in London in 1951. Candidates were judged on their face, their figure and, more and more, on their personality.

In 1968, feminist activists protested outside the Miss America pageant. They threw high heels, make-up and other "instruments of female torture" into a "Freedom Trash Can". For them, these contests reduced women to their bodies and imposed one narrow norm of beauty.

Mots clés

a canon : un modèle, une norme ; a complexion : un teint ; a pageant : un concours de beauté ; to fit the stereotype : correspondre au stéréotype.

Les normes de beauté ne sont pas seulement subies : elles sont aussi contestées et réappropriées. Ce texte présente le mouvement body positivity.

Today, images of "perfect" bodies are everywhere: on billboards, in magazines and above all on social networks, where filters can change a face in one click. Many teenagers compare themselves with these pictures, and this can damage their self-esteem.

The body positivity movement wants everybody to accept and respect their body, whatever its size, shape, skin colour or ability. Its roots go back to the fat acceptance movement of the late 1960s in the United States, but it became much more visible on social media in the 2010s, with hashtags such as #bodypositive.

Its supporters fight against body shaming, the act of mocking or criticising someone's body. Some brands now use models of different sizes and ages, and some refuse to retouch their photos.

However, the movement has its critics too. Some people say that brands only use it to sell more products. Others prefer the idea of body neutrality: instead of loving your body all the time, you simply stop judging it.

Méthode

Pour distinguer information et opinion, repère les verbes et expressions d'opinion : some people say, for them, others prefer, I think. Ce qui suit est un point de vue, pas un fait.

Les vêtements disent quelque chose de celui qui les porte : la mode peut être une manière de revendiquer une idée ou une appartenance (to make a statement).

The suffragettes' colours

At the beginning of the twentieth century, British women fought for the right to vote. In 1908, the Women's Social and Political Union, the suffragettes' organisation, chose three colours: purple for dignity, white for purity and green for hope. Supporters wore them on dresses, hats and badges so that they could recognise each other in the street.

Punk

In the 1970s in London, young punks dressed to shock: ripped T-shirts, safety pins, leather jackets, spiky hair dyed in bright colours. The designer Vivienne Westwood sold clothes for this movement in her shop on the King's Road. For many punks, looking different was a way of rejecting the norms of society.

Today

Fashion is still a way of expressing who you are. People dress up for special occasions, dress down at weekends, follow trends or ignore them completely. Choosing your outfit can be an act of creativity, of belonging to a group, or of protest.

Ces listes reprennent le lexique du programme. Apprends les mots dans les deux sens (anglais vers français et français vers anglais).

Prononciation : /θ/ et /ð/

Le th anglais se prononce la langue entre les dents : /θ/ sourd dans think, thin, both, healthy ; /ð/ sonore dans this, mother, together, clothes /kləʊðz/.

Le comparatif de supériorité

Le choix de la forme dépend de la longueur de l'adjectif :

AdjectifComparatifSuperlatif
court (1 syllabe) : talltaller thanthe tallest
consonne-voyelle-consonne : big, thinbigger, thinnerthe biggest, the thinnest
2 syllabes en -y : pretty, happyprettier, happierthe prettiest, the happiest
long (2 syllabes ou plus) : beautiful, famousmore beautiful thanthe most beautiful

Exemples : Siddal was paler than most Victorian models. Ophelia is one of the most famous paintings in Britain.

Les formes irrégulières

  • good → better → the best
  • bad → worse → the worst
  • far → farther / further → the farthest / the furthest

Égalité, infériorité et degré

  • égalité : as … as : She is as tall as her brother.
  • infériorité : not as … as ou less … than : This dress is not as expensive as that one. Superlatif : the least popular.
  • comparatif renforcé : much / far / a lot + comparatif : It is much better now. (pas very better)
  • multiplication : twice as … as, three times as … as : Her dress cost twice as much as mine.
  • progression : the + comparatif …, the + comparatif : The more you compare yourself, the less confident you feel.

Les adverbes de degré

Ils nuancent un adjectif : quite (assez), rather (plutôt), very, extremely, so, too (trop), (not) … enough (assez, placé après l'adjectif) : This outfit is quite fashionable. The jacket is not warm enough.

Attention

On dit than (que) après un comparatif, jamais that : taller than me. Après un superlatif, « de » se traduit par in devant un lieu ou un groupe : the best singer in the world, the tallest girl in the class.

sections.titre: Grammar: look, seem, appear; myself and each other
sections.html:
Look, seem, appear + adjectif

Ces verbes d'apparence sont suivis d'un adjectif, pas d'un adverbe :

  • She looks tired. (elle a l'air fatiguée) et non She looks tiredly.
  • He seems confident. (il semble sûr de lui)
  • The model appeared calm. (le mannequin paraissait calme)

Devant un nom, on emploie look like : She looks like a Pre-Raphaelite painting. Devant un verbe, on emploie seem to / appear to : He seems to know everybody.

D'autres verbes de perception fonctionnent de la même façon : to sound (That sounds great!), to feel (I feel nervous), to smell, to taste.

Les pronoms réfléchis

SujetRéfléchi
I / youmyself / yourself
he / she / ithimself / herself / itself
we / you / theyourselves / yourselves / themselves

On les emploie quand le sujet et le complément sont la même personne : She introduced herself. Teenagers compare themselves with influencers. Enjoy yourselves! Ils servent aussi à insister : I made this dress myself (moi-même).

Attention

Beaucoup de verbes pronominaux en français ne le sont pas en anglais : I get up (je me lève), she gets dressed (elle s'habille), they meet (ils se rencontrent), I feel (je me sens), to remember (se souvenir).

Le réciproque each other

Each other (ou one another) exprime une action réciproque, l'un l'autre : The two sisters looked at each other (elles se sont regardées l'une l'autre). Compare : They looked at themselves in the mirror (chacune s'est regardée elle-même).

Le gérondif est la forme verbale en -ing employée comme un nom. Il traduit souvent un infinitif ou un nom français.

En position sujet

Wearing a uniform is compulsory in many British schools. (Porter un uniforme est obligatoire…) Comparing yourself to influencers is dangerous.

En position complément

  • après une préposition, toujours : She is interested in designing clothes. Thank you for coming. He left without saying goodbye.
  • après certains verbes : enjoy, mind, avoid, finish, keep, stop, can't stand, love, like, hate : I enjoy dressing up. She can't stand being judged. Would you mind closing the door?
Attention

Dans to look forward to, to be used to, to object to, to est une préposition : I look forward to meeting you (et non to meet).

Useful phrases: describing and giving an opinion

  • In the foreground / in the background, we can see…
  • She looks… / It seems that… / It reminds me of…
  • To my mind… / As far as I'm concerned… / I'm not a huge fan of…
  • What strikes me is… / On the one hand… on the other hand…

chapitres.a_retenir:
• A beauty canon is the ideal look of a period: the Pre-Raphaelites (1848) admired pale skin and long, often red hair; beauty pageants (Miss America, 1921; Miss World, 1951) turned beauty into a competition, criticised by feminists in 1968.
  • Body positivity asks people to accept all bodies and fights body shaming; fashion can be a statement (the suffragettes' purple, white and green; punk in the 1970s).
  • Comparatif : -er than (adjectif court), more … than (adjectif long), as … as ; superlatif : the -est, the most ; irréguliers : better, the best ; worse, the worst.
  • Look, seem, appear + adjectif ; look like + nom.
  • Réfléchis : myself … themselves ; réciproque : each other.
  • Gérondif : sujet (Wearing a uniform is…), après une préposition et après enjoy, mind, avoid, can't stand.

chapitres.resume: Axe 2, Vivre entre générations : la diaspora indienne au Royaume-Uni, logement et société de classes, l'écologie comme fracture générationnelle. Grammaire : present perfect et prétérit, for/since/ago, used to et would, possessifs, quantifieurs.
chapitres.chapeau: Grandparents, parents and teenagers do not always see the world in the same way. Migration, the price of houses and climate change have transformed family life in the English-speaking world. Dans ce chapitre, tu apprends à parler du passé en lien avec le présent et à comparer les générations.
objectifs: décrire une famille et les liens entre ses membres ;
choisir entre le present perfect et le prétérit, et employer for, since et ago ;
parler d'habitudes passées avec used to et would ;
employer les possessifs (its, a friend of mine) et les quantifieurs (much, many, a few, a little) ;
présenter la diaspora indienne au Royaume-Uni, la question du logement et le débat écologique entre générations.

sections.html:
Une diaspora est l'ensemble des membres d'un peuple installés hors de leur pays d'origine. La diaspora indienne est l'une des plus importantes du monde. Lis ce texte sur les familles d'origine indienne au Royaume-Uni.

After India became independent in 1947, many Indians moved to Britain, especially in the 1950s and 1960s. They often worked in factories or in hospitals, or opened small shops. Today, people of Indian origin form one of the largest ethnic minorities in the United Kingdom, and many of them were born there.

In many British Indian families, three generations have lived under the same roof. The grandparents remember the journey from India, the parents worked hard to build a new life, and the children have grown up in Britain. They speak English at school and with friends, and sometimes Punjabi, Gujarati or Hindi at home.

These second-generation and third-generation British Indians often say that they live "between two cultures". They celebrate Diwali with their relatives and Christmas with their friends. Some of them feel pressure from their parents about their studies or their choice of partner; others feel completely at ease with both identities.

Novels and films have told these stories. In the film Bend It Like Beckham (2002), directed by Gurinder Chadha, Jess, a young British Sikh girl, dreams of playing football, while her parents would like her to follow a more traditional path.

Au Royaume-Uni, le logement révèle à la fois les différences entre générations et entre classes sociales.

For a long time, owning a house was a symbol of success in Britain. In the 1980s, the government of Margaret Thatcher introduced the Right to Buy: people who lived in council houses (social housing owned by local councils) could buy their home at a reduced price. Millions of families became home owners.

Today, the situation has changed for young people. House prices have risen much faster than salaries, so many young adults cannot afford to buy a home. They rent a flat, often for years, or they still live with their parents. Journalists call them "Generation Rent".

To buy a house, most people need a mortgage, a loan from a bank that they pay back over 25 years or more. Some young people can only buy a property with the help of their parents, or when they inherit money. For this reason, some experts say that inheritance has become more important than work in deciding who owns property.

Le changement climatique oppose-t-il les générations ? Le texte présente deux points de vue.

In 2018, the Swedish teenager Greta Thunberg started a school strike for the climate. Her movement, Fridays for Future, quickly spread to the English-speaking world: in 2019, hundreds of thousands of students walked out of their classes in Britain, Australia and the United States.

Many young activists blame older generations, sometimes called the "boomers", for decades of greenhouse gas emissions. The expression "OK, boomer" became popular online in 2019 to dismiss older people's opinions.

But the reality is more complex. Surveys show that many older people are also worried about climate change, and some of them have joined climate groups created by grandparents. On the other hand, not all young people are activists. For many experts, the real divide is less between generations than between rich and poor, or between those who can and those who cannot change their way of life.

EnglishFrançais

to rent / to letlouer (en tant que locataire) / louer (en tant que propriétaire)

Environment

EnglishFrançais
greenhouse gas emissionsles émissions de gaz à effet de serre
to cut emissionsréduire les émissions
renewables, green energyles énergies renouvelables
wind turbines / solar panelsles éoliennes / les panneaux solaires
to phase outabandonner progressivement
environmentally friendlyrespectueux de l'environnement
a tipping pointun point de bascule
to litterjeter des déchets par terre

Le prétérit : un passé coupé du présent

Le prétérit (worked, went) présente un fait terminé, situé à un moment précis du passé : India became independent in 1947. They moved to Britain in the 1960s. Il s'emploie avec yesterday, last year, in 2019, two years ago, when I was a child.

Le present perfect : un passé lié au présent

Il se forme avec have / has + participe passé : I have lived, she has grown, they haven't seen. Il présente un fait passé à travers ses conséquences ou son bilan dans le présent :

  • bilan, expérience : Have you ever been to India? (sans date) ;
  • conséquence actuelle : House prices have risen (ils sont plus élevés aujourd'hui) ;
  • action qui dure jusqu'à maintenant : She has lived in Leicester for ten years (elle y vit toujours).
Attention

Le français dit « J'habite ici depuis dix ans » au présent ; l'anglais emploie le present perfect : I have lived here for ten years, jamais I live here since… Et une date ou ago impose le prétérit : I saw her two days ago, jamais I have seen her two days ago.

For, since, ago

MotSensExemple
for + duréedepuis, pendant (une durée)for three years, for a long time
since + point de départdepuis (une date, un moment)since 2018, since I was ten, since Monday
durée + agoil y a (avec le prétérit)two days ago, a long time ago

Pour insister sur l'activité qui dure, on emploie le present perfect be + -ing : They have been waiting for a council flat for two years.

Questions utiles : How long have you lived here? (depuis combien de temps) ; When did you arrive? (quand).

Used to + base verbale

Used to exprime une habitude ou un état passés qui ne sont plus vrais aujourd'hui. Il se traduit souvent par l'imparfait :

  • My grandparents used to live in Mumbai. (ils habitaient, ils n'y habitent plus)
  • négation : I didn't use to like spicy food.
  • question : Did you use to walk to school?

Would + base verbale

Would peut aussi exprimer une action répétée dans le passé, surtout dans un récit de souvenirs : Every Sunday, my grandmother would cook for the whole family. Mais would ne s'emploie pas pour un état : on dit She used to have long hair, pas She would have long hair.

Ne pas confondre

to be used to + V-ing / nom signifie « être habitué à » : She is used to living between two cultures. Ici to est une préposition, d'où le gérondif.

Les possessifs

Déterminant (devant un nom)Pronom (seul)
my, your, his, her, its, our, theirmine, yours, his, hers, —, ours, theirs
  • Le possessif s'accorde avec le possesseur, pas avec l'objet : Jess and her father (son père à elle), Tom and his mother (sa mère à lui).
  • its (sans apostrophe) est le possessif d'une chose ou d'un animal : The movement has its critics. it's = it is ou it has : It's raining.
  • a friend of mine = un de mes amis ; a cousin of hers = une de ses cousines (à elle).

Les quantifieurs

Dénombrable (people, houses)Indénombrable (money, time, advice)
beaucoupmany (a lot of)much (a lot of)
quelques, un peu (sens positif)a fewa little
peu (sens négatif)fewlittle
combienhow manyhow much

Exemples : Few young people can afford a house (peu, presque aucun). She has a few friends in London (quelques-uns). There is little hope (peu d'espoir). We have a little time (un peu de temps).

Some s'emploie surtout à la forme affirmative, any à la forme négative et interrogative : Have you got any brothers? I haven't got any. Les structures partitives : some of them, most of us, all of my relatives.

chapitres.a_retenir:
• After 1947, many Indians settled in Britain; their children and grandchildren often live between two cultures.
  • Generation Rent: house prices have risen faster than salaries, so many young people rent instead of buying; a mortgage is a loan to buy a house.
  • Climate change is sometimes presented as a generational divide (Fridays for Future, "OK, boomer"), but many experts point to inequalities of wealth.
  • Prétérit : fait passé daté et terminé (in 1947, two years ago) ; present perfect (have + participe passé) : bilan ou action qui dure jusqu'à maintenant.
  • for + durée, since + point de départ, durée + ago (avec le prétérit).
  • used to + base verbale : habitude ou état passés révolus ; would : action répétée dans un récit (pas un état).
  • its = possessif, it's = it is ; many / a few / few + dénombrable, much / a little / little + indénombrable.

chapitres.resume: Axe 3, Le passé dans le présent : la culture aborigène dans l'Australie contemporaine, les commissions de réconciliation en Afrique du Sud et au Canada, les statues et les monuments. Grammaire : prétérit simple et be + -ing, le passif, les propositions relatives.
chapitres.chapeau: Monuments, traditions and memories connect us with the past. Some countries have also had to face the darkest pages of their history in order to live together. Dans ce chapitre, tu apprends à raconter des événements passés et à comprendre des textes qui utilisent le passif et les relatives.
objectifs: raconter des événements passés avec le prétérit simple et le prétérit be + -ing ;
reconnaître et former la voix passive ;
relier des idées avec les pronoms relatifs who, which, that, whose et whom ;
employer le vocabulaire de l'héritage, de la mémoire, du danger et de la protection ;
présenter la culture aborigène, les commissions de réconciliation et le débat sur les monuments.

sections.html:
Les Aborigènes et les insulaires du détroit de Torres sont les premiers habitants de l'Australie. Ce texte présente leur place dans l'Australie d'aujourd'hui.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived in Australia for at least 50,000 years. Their cultures are often described as the oldest continuous living cultures in the world. They are made of hundreds of different nations and languages, and they share a deep connection with the land, which is expressed in stories, songs, dances and paintings.

When the British arrived in 1788, they treated the land as if it belonged to nobody. Aboriginal people lost their lands, and many died of violence and disease. Between about 1910 and the 1970s, thousands of Aboriginal children were taken from their families by the authorities and placed in institutions or with white families. These children are known as the Stolen Generations.

On 13 February 2008, Prime Minister Kevin Rudd made a formal National Apology to the Stolen Generations in the Australian Parliament. He said "sorry" three times on behalf of the nation.

Uluru, a huge red rock in the centre of the country, is a sacred site for its traditional owners, the Anangu people. For decades, tourists climbed it, although the Anangu asked them not to. Since October 2019, climbing Uluru has been forbidden.

Comment vivre ensemble après des violences graves ? Plusieurs pays anglophones ont créé des commissions de vérité et de réconciliation.

South Africa

From 1948 to the early 1990s, South Africa was ruled by apartheid, a system of racial segregation that kept Black South Africans apart and deprived them of their rights. After Nelson Mandela became the first Black president in 1994, the new government set up the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu. It began its work in 1996.

Victims came to testify in public hearings, which were broadcast on radio and television. People who had committed political crimes could ask for amnesty if they told the whole truth. The aim was not revenge but understanding, so that the nation could move forward.

Canada

In Canada, more than 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children were sent to residential schools, boarding schools run by churches and funded by the government. The children were separated from their families and often forbidden to speak their own languages. Many suffered abuse. The last schools closed in the 1990s.

Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission worked from 2008 to 2015. It listened to thousands of survivors and published 94 "Calls to Action" to repair the damage. Since 2021, 30 September has been the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

Les monuments rendent hommage à des personnes ou à des événements. Mais que faire quand l'histoire d'un personnage honoré est contestée ?

Statues are built to commemorate people that a society admires. Over time, however, opinions change. In June 2020, during protests in Bristol, England, the statue of Edward Colston was pulled down and thrown into the harbour. Colston was a seventeenth-century merchant who had made a fortune from the slave trade. He had also given money to many schools and charities in the city.

The statue was later taken out of the water, and it is now displayed in a museum, lying down, with the protesters' placards next to it. For some people, removing such statues erases history. For others, it is history which explains them: a statue is not a history lesson but a tribute, and a museum is a better place to tell the whole story.

Other monuments are built to remember the victims of the past. In London, the Cenotaph, a war memorial in Whitehall, is the centre of the national ceremony of Remembrance Sunday every November.

Méthode

Dans un texte d'opinion, repère les connecteurs qui introduisent les arguments opposés : for some people… for others…, however, but. Résumer, c'est rendre les deux points de vue sans prendre parti.

sections.titre: Grammar: the preterite, simple and be + -ing
sections.html:
Le prétérit simple

Il raconte des faits passés et terminés. Verbes réguliers : base + -ed (arrived, apologised, stopped). Verbes irréguliers : forme à apprendre (go → went, take → took, make → made, give → gave, build → built, lose → lost).

Négation et question avec did + base verbale : They did not (didn't) ask permission. When did the British arrive?

Le prétérit be + -ing

Formé avec was / were + V-ing, il présente une action en cours à un moment du passé. Il sert souvent de décor à une action ponctuelle au prétérit simple :

  • Protesters were marching through Bristol when they pulled down the statue.
  • While the commission was listening to survivors, journalists were taking notes. (deux actions en cours en même temps)
Attention

when introduit souvent l'action ponctuelle (prétérit simple), while l'action en cours (be + -ing). Les verbes d'état (know, like, belong, want) ne se mettent pas à la forme be + -ing : They knew the truth.

Le pluperfect (en reconnaissance)

had + participe passé marque une action antérieure à une autre action passée : Colston had made a fortune before he gave money to schools.

À la voix passive, le sujet subit l'action. On la forme avec be, conjugué au temps voulu, + participe passé. Le complément d'agent est introduit par by.

TempsActifPassif
présentThousands of tourists visit Uluru.Uluru is visited by thousands of tourists.
prétéritThe authorities took the children.The children were taken by the authorities.
present perfectThey have closed the schools.The schools have been closed.
avec un modalWe must protect this site.This site must be protected.

On emploie le passif quand l'agent est inconnu, évident ou peu important, ou pour mettre en valeur ce qui subit l'action : The statue was pulled down in 2020. Le français emploie souvent « on » : English is spoken here (on parle anglais ici).

Avec les verbes à deux compléments, le sujet du passif est souvent la personne : The victims were given a voice. She was told the truth.

Une proposition relative complète un nom (l'antécédent). Le pronom relatif dépend de l'antécédent et de sa fonction :

PronomEmploiExemple
whopersonne, sujet (ou complément à l'oral)the man who chaired the commission
whompersonne, complément (langue soutenue, après une préposition)the survivors to whom the Prime Minister apologised
whichchose, animala rock which is sacred
thatpersonne ou chose, dans une relative déterminativethe statue that was pulled down
whosepossession : dont le / la / lesa nation whose children were taken
where / whenlieu / tempsthe city where he lived ; the day when she testified

Relative déterminative et relative explicative

  • La déterminative est indispensable pour identifier l'antécédent ; pas de virgules : The children who were taken never forgot. Le relatif complément peut être omis : the museum (that) we visited.
  • L'explicative ajoute une information ; elle est entre virgules et n'accepte ni that ni l'omission : Desmond Tutu, who was an archbishop, chaired the commission.
Attention

Which peut reprendre toute une proposition : The hearings were broadcast, which helped people understand. (ce qui a aidé…)

chapitres.a_retenir:
• Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures are among the oldest living cultures; the Stolen Generations were children taken from their families; the National Apology was made on 13 February 2008; climbing Uluru has been forbidden since 2019.
  • South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (chaired by Desmond Tutu, from 1996) and Canada's (2008–2015, on residential schools) listened to victims to help the nation live together.
  • Statues commemorate; some, like Edward Colston's in Bristol (2020), are contested.
  • Prétérit simple : fait passé terminé (did pour la négation et la question) ; prétérit was / were + V-ing : action en cours dans le passé.
  • Passif : be au temps voulu + participe passé (+ by agent).
  • Relatifs : who (personne), which (chose), that (déterminative), whose (dont, possession), whom (personne complément, soutenu).

chapitres.resume: Axe 4, Défis et transitions : des syndicats aux hashtags, le métro de Londres et la ville, la consommation et le recyclage. Grammaire : l'expression du futur, les conditionnelles, les modaux de probabilité, les connecteurs logiques.
chapitres.chapeau: How do people come together to change society? How are our cities and our habits changing? From nineteenth-century trade unions to online movements, from the first Tube line to fast fashion, this chapter looks at challenges and transitions in the English-speaking world. Tu apprends à parler de l'avenir, à faire des hypothèses et à argumenter.
objectifs: parler de l'avenir avec will, be going to et le présent be + -ing ;
formuler des hypothèses et des conditions avec if et unless ;
exprimer des degrés de probabilité avec may, might, must et can't ;
articuler un argument avec des connecteurs d'opposition, de concession et de conséquence ;
présenter des formes de mobilisation, l'histoire du métro de Londres et les enjeux de la consommation.

sections.html:
Comment les citoyens s'organisent-ils pour défendre leurs droits ? Ce texte suit l'évolution des formes de mobilisation dans le monde anglophone.

The Tolpuddle Martyrs

In 1834, six farm workers from the village of Tolpuddle, in Dorset, England, formed a trade union to protest against their very low wages. They were arrested and sentenced to transportation to Australia for seven years. Huge protests followed and a petition was signed by hundreds of thousands of people. The men were pardoned in 1836. Today, they are remembered as the Tolpuddle Martyrs, pioneers of the trade union movement.

The suffragettes

In 1903, Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women's Social and Political Union. Its motto was "Deeds, not words". The suffragettes organised marches, chained themselves to railings and broke windows; many were sent to prison. In 1918, some women over 30 won the right to vote, and in 1928 women finally voted on the same terms as men.

Hashtag activism

Today, many movements start online. #BlackLivesMatter was created in 2013 by three activists, Alicia Garza, Patrisse Cullors and Opal Tometi, to protest against racism and police violence. In 2017, millions of women used #MeToo, a phrase first used by the activist Tarana Burke in 2006, to share their experiences of sexual harassment.

Social networks make it easier to build a movement quickly. But critics say that clicking "like" is not the same as being committed: they call it "slacktivism". Online campaigns can also spread rumours and fake news. Most successful movements combine online campaigns and people in the streets.

Les transports transforment l'organisation des villes. L'exemple du métro de Londres montre comment une innovation change un espace urbain.

On 10 January 1863, the world's first underground railway opened in London, between Paddington and Farringdon. The trains were pulled by steam engines, so the tunnels were full of smoke. Londoners soon called their underground railway "the Tube". It enabled people to live further from the centre and to travel to work every day: the suburbs grew quickly along the new lines.

In 1933, Harry Beck, an engineering draughtsman, designed a new map of the Underground. Instead of showing real distances, it used straight lines and regular spaces, like an electrical circuit. His idea was so clear that it has inspired transport maps all over the world.

Today, cities face new challenges: more people, more traffic and air pollution. London introduced an Ultra Low Emission Zone in 2019: drivers of the most polluting vehicles must pay a daily charge. Cities are also building cycle lanes and new lines, such as the Elizabeth line, which opened in 2022. Will the city of the future be a city without cars? Some urban planners believe it will; others think that electric cars will simply replace petrol ones.

Que deviennent les objets que nous achetons ? Ce texte interroge la société de consommation et ses alternatives.

After the Second World War, the consumer society developed quickly in the United States and in Britain. For many people, owning a car, a television and a fridge was part of the American Dream. Growth seemed unlimited.

Today, we buy more clothes than ever. Fast fashion brands produce new collections every few weeks at very low prices. But this has a cost: clothes are often made in poor countries, in factories called sweatshops, where workers are badly paid. In April 2013, the Rana Plaza building collapsed in Bangladesh and more than 1,100 garment workers died. The disaster made many consumers ask: who made my clothes?

Alternatives are growing. People buy second-hand clothes in charity shops or thrift shops, on apps and websites, and choose refurbished phones. Others repair objects instead of throwing them away. Some governments act too: since October 2015, shops in England have had to charge for single-use plastic bags, and the number of bags used has fallen dramatically.

However, recycling alone will not solve the problem. As many environmentalists say: the best waste is the waste we don't produce.

Mobilisation

EnglishFrançais
a trade unionun syndicat
a strike / to go on strikeune grève / faire grève
a demonstration / to demonstrate againstune manifestation / manifester contre
a placard, a signune pancarte
to take part in, to participate inparticiper à
to be committed / to be involvedêtre engagé / être impliqué
to build a movementconstruire un mouvement
to come togetherse rassembler
to pledgepromettre, s'engager solennellement
to spread rumoursrépandre des rumeurs
fake newsles fausses informations
biased / impartialpartial, orienté / impartial

Scientific discoveries

EnglishFrançais
a breakthroughune percée, une avancée décisive
a findingun résultat (de recherche)
groundbreaking, trailblazingrévolutionnaire, pionnier
state-of-the-artde pointe, dernier cri
to enablepermettre, rendre possible
to unveil / to uncoverdévoiler / découvrir, mettre au jour
to stumble upontomber par hasard sur
the Industrial Revolutionla révolution industrielle

Consumption

EnglishFrançais
consumption / over-consumptionla consommation / la surconsommation
to affordavoir les moyens de
cheap / expensive, priceybon marché / cher
second-hand / refurbishedd'occasion / reconditionné
waste / to waste / to throw awayles déchets, le gaspillage / gaspiller / jeter
a sweatshopun atelier où les ouvriers sont exploités
to cut down onréduire (sa consommation de)
a charity shop, a thrift shopune boutique solidaire, une friperie
Faux amis

a manifestation n'est pas une manifestation de rue (on dit a demonstration, a protest) ; actually signifie « en fait », et non « actuellement » (currently, nowadays).

L'anglais n'a pas de temps « futur » : il utilise plusieurs formes, selon la manière dont on voit l'avenir.

FormeEmploiExemple
will + base verbaleprédiction, décision prise sur le moment, promesseCities will be greener in 2050. I'll help you!
be going to + base verbaleintention déjà décidée ; prévision fondée sur un indice présentI'm going to buy second-hand clothes. Look at the sky: it's going to rain.
présent be + -ingaction prévue, organisée (avec une date)We're meeting the union leaders tomorrow.
présent simplehoraire, programme officielThe train leaves at 8.15.

Négation : will not → won't ; I'm not going to. Question : Will you come? Are you going to sign the petition?

Attention

Après when, as soon as, before, until au sens temporel, on emploie le présent, pas will : I'll call you when I arrive (et non when I will arrive).

La condition réalisable

if + présent, will + base verbale : If we cut emissions, the planet will be healthier. On n'emploie jamais will juste après if.

L'hypothèse (irréel du présent)

if + prétérit, would + base verbale : If cities banned cars, the air would be cleaner. Avec be, on emploie souvent were à toutes les personnes : If I were the mayor, I would build more cycle lanes. Le prétérit après if n'exprime pas le passé mais l'irréel.

Unless

unless = if … not (à moins que, sauf si) : Unless we act now, it will be too late = If we don't act now, …

L'irréel du passé (en reconnaissance)

if + pluperfect, would have + participe passé : If the workers had been paid more, they wouldn't have formed a union. Dans la langue soutenue, on peut inverser le sujet et supprimer if : Had she known, she would have stayed (si elle avait su…).

Les modaux de probabilité

Ils expriment le degré de certitude de celui qui parle :

ModalDegréExemple
mustquasi-certitude (déduction)The streets are wet: it must have rained. She must be exhausted.
willprédiction sûrePrices will rise.
shouldforte probabilitéThe new line should open next year.
maypossibilité (environ une chance sur deux)Electric cars may replace petrol cars.
might, couldpossibilité plus faibleIt might snow tomorrow.
can'tquasi-impossibilité (déduction)That can't be true!

Les modaux sont suivis de la base verbale, sans to, et ne prennent pas de -s : It may be true (et non It mays be). Pour une déduction sur le passé : modal + have + participe passé.

Les connecteurs logiques

FonctionConnecteurs
ajoutermoreover, besides, what's more, in addition
opposerbut, however, whereas, while, on the one hand… on the other hand
concéderalthough, even though, yet, in spite of / despite + nom ou V-ing
causebecause, since, as, because of + nom
conséquenceso, therefore, consequently, as a result
illustrerfor example, for instance, such as, like

Exemple : Fast fashion is cheap. However, it has a high human cost. Although recycling helps, it is not enough; therefore, we should buy less.

Attention

despite et in spite of sont suivis d'un nom ou d'un gérondif, jamais d'une proposition : Despite the rain, they marched ; mais Although it was raining, they marched.

chapitres.a_retenir:
• Mobilisation: the Tolpuddle Martyrs (1834) formed a trade union; the suffragettes ("Deeds, not words") fought for the vote; online movements such as #BlackLivesMatter (2013) and #MeToo (2017) spread quickly.
  • The London Underground opened in 1863; Harry Beck's map (1933) was a model for the world; today cities fight pollution (ULEZ, 2019).
  • Fast fashion and sweatshops (Rana Plaza, 2013) raise questions; alternatives: second-hand, refurbished, repairing.
  • Futur : will (prédiction, décision immédiate), be going to (intention, indice présent), présent be + -ing (action organisée).
  • if + présent → will ; if + prétérit → would ; unless = if … not.
  • Probabilité : must (quasi sûr), may, might (possible), can't (quasi impossible).
  • Connecteurs : however, whereas (opposition), although, despite (concession), therefore, as a result (conséquence).

chapitres.resume: Axe 5, Créer et recréer : le mythe du cowboy, la légende de Robin Hood, les adaptations de Romeo and Juliet et la machine hollywoodienne. Grammaire : le discours indirect, les phrasal verbs, le but et le moyen, les exclamatives et les causatives.
chapitres.chapeau: Some stories never die: they are told again and again, in ballads, novels, films and songs. Each new version says something about the period that creates it. Dans ce chapitre, tu découvres comment mythes, légendes et classiques sont recréés, et tu apprends à raconter une intrigue, à rapporter des paroles et à donner ton avis sur une œuvre.
objectifs: raconter l'intrigue d'une œuvre et donner un avis argumenté ;
rapporter des paroles au discours indirect ;
employer des phrasal verbs courants ;
exprimer le but et le moyen, et formuler des exclamatives ;
présenter le mythe du cowboy, la légende de Robin Hood, les adaptations de Romeo and Juliet et Hollywood.

sections.titre: The cowboy: from history to myth
sections.html:
Le cowboy est l'une des grandes figures de la culture américaine. Mais le personnage du mythe ressemble-t-il aux cowboys réels ?

After the American Civil War (1861–1865), cowboys drove huge herds of cattle from Texas to the railway towns of Kansas, where the animals were sent to cities in the East. These cattle drives lasted several months. The work was hard, dangerous and badly paid. Historians estimate that about one cowboy in four was Black, and many others were Mexican vaqueros, who had taught the Americans many of their skills.

Yet the cowboy of the myth is usually a lonely white hero who fights for justice with his gun. This image was created by popular novels and shows, such as Buffalo Bill's Wild West, which toured America and Europe from 1883. Then Hollywood turned it into a genre: the western. In films like Stagecoach (1939), by John Ford, John Wayne became the face of the courageous, independent cowboy.

Since then, artists have kept recreating the myth. Some westerns showed Native Americans as victims rather than villains; others questioned the cowboy's masculinity, like Brokeback Mountain (2005). In 2024, the singer Beyoncé released Cowboy Carter, an album which reclaims the Black roots of country music.

Une légende change avec chaque époque qui la raconte. Robin Hood en est un bon exemple.

Robin Hood first appeared in English ballads in the late Middle Ages. In these songs, he is an outlaw who lives in Sherwood Forest, near Nottingham, with his "merry men", among them Little John and Friar Tuck. His enemy is the Sheriff of Nottingham. Nobody knows if he really existed.

Over the centuries, the story was rewritten many times. Later versions made Robin a nobleman who had lost his lands, added the character of Maid Marian, and turned him into the hero who "robs from the rich to give to the poor".

Cinema gave the legend new faces: the swashbuckling Errol Flynn in The Adventures of Robin Hood (1938), a fox in Disney's animated film (1973), Kevin Costner in Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves (1991). Each version reflects its time: in some, Robin is a romantic adventurer; in others, he is a rebel fighting against an unfair government. That is how a legend survives: by adapting itself to new audiences.

sections.titre: Romeo and Juliet, again and again
sections.html:
Les grandes œuvres classiques se déclinent au fil des époques. Romeo and Juliet a été adapté sur scène, à l'écran et en musique.

William Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet in the mid-1590s. In Verona, two young people fall in love although their families, the Montagues and the Capulets, hate each other. Their secret marriage ends in tragedy: both lovers die. The play is so famous that "a Romeo" has become a common noun for a passionate lover.

In 1957, the musical West Side Story moved the story to New York. The rival families became two street gangs, the Jets and the Sharks, a white gang and a Puerto Rican gang. The film version won ten Oscars in 1962, and Steven Spielberg directed a new adaptation in 2021. In 1996, Baz Luhrmann's film Romeo + Juliet, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Claire Danes, kept Shakespeare's language but set the story in a modern city, with guns instead of swords.

Hollywood tells its own story

Hollywood also likes to put itself on screen. Singin' in the Rain (1952) shows the difficult transition from silent films to "talkies" in the late 1920s. More recent films, such as La La Land (2016), tell the dreams and disappointments of young artists in Los Angeles. In this way, the "dream factory" builds its own myth, which is also a powerful form of soft power.

Creation and storytelling

EnglishFrançais
a plotune intrigue
a character / the main characterun personnage / le personnage principal
a playwright / a novelistun dramaturge / un romancier
a play / a novel / a balladune pièce de théâtre / un roman / une ballade
a remake / an adaptationune nouvelle version d'un film / une adaptation
to be set inse dérouler à / dans
to direct / a directorréaliser / un réalisateur
to star / starringjouer le rôle principal / avec (au générique)
to cast / the castattribuer les rôles / la distribution
a cliffhangerun suspense de fin d'épisode
a happy endingune fin heureuse
storytellingl'art de raconter des histoires
an outlawun hors-la-loi
to craftfaçonner, créer avec soin

Giving your opinion on a work

  • It's a must-see. / It's worth seeing. / It's not worth reading.
  • The plot is gripping / predictable. The acting is convincing / disappointing.
  • What I liked most was… / I was moved by… / I found it boring because…
Faux amis

a novel = un roman (une nouvelle se dit a short story) ; a location = un lieu de tournage (une location se dit a rental).

Le discours indirect rapporte les paroles de quelqu'un sans les citer. Quand le verbe introducteur est au passé (said, told, asked), les temps reculent d'un cran :

Discours directDiscours indirect
présent : "I love westerns."He said (that) he loved westerns.
present perfect : "I have seen the film."She said she had seen the film.
prétérit : "We met in Verona."They said they had met in Verona.
will : "I will marry her."Romeo said he would marry her.
can : "I can help."He said he could help.

Les repères changent aussi : today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before, here → there, this → that, now → then.

Say ou tell ?

tell est suivi de la personne à qui l'on parle : He told me (that) he was tired. say n'est pas suivi directement de la personne : He said (that) he was tired ou He said to me…

Questions et ordres

  • question fermée : if / whether : "Are you coming?" → She asked if I was coming.
  • question ouverte : mot interrogatif, puis ordre sujet-verbe, sans do : "Where do you live?" → He asked me where I lived.
  • ordre : tell / ask sb (not) to + base verbale : "Don't move!" → The sheriff told him not to move.

Ce recul de will à would exprime le futur dans le passé : She knew that she would become an actress.

Un phrasal verb associe un verbe et une particule (up, out, off, down, on…). Le sens de l'ensemble est souvent différent de celui du verbe seul.

Phrasal verbSensExemple
give upabandonner, renoncer àNever give up your dreams.
look forward to + V-ingattendre avec impatienceI look forward to seeing the remake.
find outdécouvrir (une information)She found out the truth.
figure outcomprendre, trouver (la solution)I can't figure out the ending.
come up withtrouver, avoir (une idée)He came up with a new version.
turn downrefuser (une offre) ; baisser (le son)She turned down the role.
put offrepousser, reporterThey put off the premiere.
get byse débrouillerCowboys got by on very little money.
cheer upremonter le moral, reprendre courageCheer up! It's only a film.
set upcréer, fonderThey set up a film studio.
bring upélever ; aborder (un sujet)He was brought up in Texas.
take offdécoller ; connaître un succès soudain ; enlever (un vêtement)Her career took off in 2016.

Avec un pronom complément, les phrasal verbs séparables placent le pronom entre le verbe et la particule : She turned it down (et non She turned down it).

Le but

  • to + base verbale : He moved to Hollywood to become an actor.
  • in order to / so as to + base verbale (plus soutenu) ; négation : in order not to, so as not to : She left early so as not to miss the start.
  • so that + sujet + modal : They wore green so that people could recognise them.
Attention

On ne dit jamais for to : « pour voir » se traduit to see, et non for see ni for to see.

Le moyen

by + V-ing (en faisant) : A legend survives by adapting itself to new audiences.

Les exclamatives

  • What a / an + (adjectif +) nom singulier dénombrable : What a beautiful story!
  • What + (adjectif +) nom pluriel ou indénombrable : What wonderful actors! What terrible weather!
  • How + adjectif ou adverbe : How sad the ending is! How well she sings!
  • so + adjectif, such (a) + nom : It was so moving! It was such a moving film!

Les causatives

  • make sb do (faire faire, contraindre) : The film made me cry.
  • let sb do (laisser faire, permettre) : Her parents didn't let her play football.
  • au passif, make reprend to : He was made to leave.

chapitres.a_retenir:
• Real cowboys drove cattle after the Civil War; about one in four was Black; the myth was built by Buffalo Bill's show (1883) and westerns (John Wayne), then questioned and reclaimed.
  • Robin Hood, the outlaw of Sherwood Forest, comes from medieval ballads; every period has retold the legend in its own way.
  • Romeo and Juliet (Shakespeare, 1590s) was adapted as West Side Story (1957) and by Baz Luhrmann (1996); Hollywood also tells its own story (Singin' in the Rain).
  • Discours indirect : recul des temps (loves → loved, will → would), tell sb / say, asked if…, told him to….
  • Phrasal verbs : give up, find out, come up with, turn down ; pronom placé avant la particule (turn it down).
  • But : to / in order to / so as to + base verbale ; moyen : by + V-ing.
  • Exclamatives : What a …!, How …! ; causatives : make sb do, let sb do.

chapitres.resume: Axe 6, Les pays du Commonwealth (axe obligatoire) : de l'Empire au Commonwealth, le Commonwealth aujourd'hui, les voix de la littérature et la génération Windrush. Grammaire : modaux d'obligation et de capacité, wish et le regret, question tags et réponses courtes, groupe nominal complexe et démonstratifs.
chapitres.chapeau: The Commonwealth of Nations brings together 56 countries on every continent, most of them former parts of the British Empire. What do they still share, and how do they assert their own identities? Ce chapitre, obligatoire dans le programme, retrace le passage de l'Empire au Commonwealth et te fait entendre des voix venues de ses pays.
objectifs: exprimer l'obligation, l'absence d'obligation, l'interdiction et la capacité ;
exprimer un souhait ou un regret avec wish ;
utiliser les question tags et les réponses courtes ;
construire des groupes nominaux complexes et choisir le bon démonstratif ;
présenter l'histoire et les institutions du Commonwealth, la génération Windrush et des écrivains qui en sont issus.

sections.html:
Comment l'Empire britannique, le plus vaste de l'histoire, s'est-il transformé en une association libre de pays égaux ?

At its peak, in the early twentieth century, the British Empire ruled about a quarter of the world's population. People used to say that "the sun never set" on it. But some of its territories were already moving towards self-government. Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa became dominions, and in 1931 the Statute of Westminster recognised their independence from the British Parliament.

After the Second World War, the Empire began to break up. In 1947, British India was divided into two independent states, India and Pakistan; the partition caused terrible violence and forced millions of people to leave their homes. In 1957, Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence. Many others followed in the 1960s, such as Nigeria (1960), Jamaica (1962) and Kenya (1963), sometimes after violent conflicts.

In 1949, the London Declaration created the modern Commonwealth. It allowed India to stay a member even though it was becoming a republic: members would be "free and equal", and the King would simply be the symbol of their association, as Head of the Commonwealth.

Le Commonwealth d'aujourd'hui est une organisation volontaire, très diverse, dont les liens sont autant culturels que politiques.

Today, the Commonwealth has 56 member states with about 2.7 billion people, a third of the world's population. Most of its members are former British territories, but not all of them: Mozambique (1995) and Rwanda (2009) joined without any colonial link with Britain, and so did Gabon and Togo in 2022. Being a member does not depend on the British monarchy: Barbados became a republic in 2021 and remained in the Commonwealth.

Since 2022, King Charles III has been Head of the Commonwealth. He is also the head of state of 15 Commonwealth realms, among them the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Jamaica. In the other member states, the head of state is a president or a local monarch. The organisation is run by a Secretariat based at Marlborough House, in London.

Members share values written in the Commonwealth Charter (2013): democracy, human rights and the rule of law. They cooperate on trade, education and climate change, which threatens many small island states. Every four years, athletes meet at the Commonwealth Games, first held in Hamilton, Canada, in 1930 as the British Empire Games. Commonwealth Day is celebrated on the second Monday in March.

La littérature anglophone des pays du Commonwealth raconte l'histoire, et des histoires, du point de vue de ceux qui l'ont vécue.

Writers

  • Chinua Achebe (Nigeria) published Things Fall Apart in 1958. The novel describes life in an Igbo village before and after the arrival of British missionaries and colonial rulers. It wanted to show Africa from an African point of view.
  • Salman Rushdie (India / UK) won the Booker Prize for Midnight's Children (1981), whose hero is born at the exact moment India becomes independent.
  • Arundhati Roy (India) won the Booker Prize in 1997 for The God of Small Things, set in Kerala.
  • Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie (Nigeria) warned against "the danger of a single story" in a famous 2009 talk: if we only hear one story about a country, we create stereotypes.

The Windrush generation

On 22 June 1948, the ship HMT Empire Windrush arrived at Tilbury, near London, with hundreds of passengers from the Caribbean. Britain needed workers to rebuild the country after the war, and citizens of the colonies had the right to settle in the UK. Those who came between 1948 and the early 1970s are called the Windrush generation.

In 2018, the "Windrush scandal" revealed that some of them had been wrongly treated as illegal immigrants, and some had even been deported. The government apologised. Since 2018, 22 June has been celebrated as Windrush Day, to honour the contribution of Caribbean migrants to British society.

Prononciation : le suffixe -ate

Il se prononce /eɪt/ dans un verbe (to celebrate, to separate, to graduate) et souvent /ət/ ou /ɪt/ dans un nom ou un adjectif (a graduate, separate, private).

SensFormeExemple
obligation (vue par celui qui parle)mustYou must respect the rules.
obligation (extérieure, règle)have toMembers have to share the values of the Charter.
interdictionmustn't, can't, be not allowed toYou mustn't smoke here.
absence d'obligationdon't have to, needn'tYou don't have to be a former colony to join.
conseil, devoir moralshould, ought toThe government ought to apologise.
capacitécan, be able toShe can speak three languages.
permissioncan, may, be allowed toMay I come in?
Attention

mustn't signifie « il ne faut pas » (interdiction), alors que don't have to signifie « ce n'est pas la peine » (pas d'obligation). Ces deux formes ne sont jamais équivalentes.

Les autres temps : les formes périphrastiques

must et can n'ont pas de futur ni de present perfect. On emploie have to et be able to :

  • passé : Many people had to leave their homes in 1947. She was able to escape.
  • futur : Small islands will have to adapt. One day, we will be able to…
  • present perfect : They have had to wait for years.

Au passif, on peut exprimer la contrainte avec be made to : They were made to leave.

sections.titre: Grammar: wish, question tags, short answers
sections.html:
Wish : le souhait et le regret

  • wish + prétérit : regret sur le présent (si seulement…) : I wish I spoke Hindi (je regrette de ne pas parler hindi). Avec be : I wish I were in Jamaica.
  • wish + pluperfect : regret sur le passé : She wishes she had stayed in Kingston (elle regrette d'être partie).
  • wish + would : souhait que quelqu'un d'autre change : I wish the media would talk about it.
  • If only… fonctionne de la même façon, avec plus d'intensité : If only I had known!

Les question tags

Un tag est une courte question en fin de phrase (« n'est-ce pas ? »). Il reprend l'auxiliaire de la phrase et inverse la polarité :

  • phrase affirmative → tag négatif : Jamaica is a realm, isn't it? You have read Achebe, haven't you?
  • phrase négative → tag affirmatif : You don't know him, do you? She can't come, can she?
  • sans auxiliaire, on emploie do / does / did : He arrived in 1948, didn't he?
  • cas particuliers : I'm right, aren't I? Let's go, shall we?

Les réponses courtes

On répond par yes / no + sujet + auxiliaire, sans répéter le verbe : Have you been to India? — Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. Does she live in Lagos? — Yes, she does. On réagit de la même façon : I love this novel. — So do I. (moi aussi) I can't swim. — Neither can I. (moi non plus)

Le groupe nominal complexe

En anglais, le nom principal est placé à la fin du groupe ; ce qui le précède le caractérise.

StructureExempleTraduction
nom + noma member state, a war memorial, a teacupun État membre, un monument aux morts, une tasse à thé
N's N (génitif) : le possesseur est une personne, un pays, une duréethe King's role, India's independence, a day's workle rôle du roi, l'indépendance de l'Inde, une journée de travail
N of N : contenu, quantité, partiea cup of tea, a pair of shoes, the end of the Empireune tasse de thé, une paire de chaussures, la fin de l'Empire
génitif génériquea children's book, a women's magazineun livre pour enfants, un magazine féminin

Dans un nom composé, le premier nom reste au singulier : a five-year plan, a 56-member organisation. Pour un pluriel en -s, le génitif s'écrit avec la seule apostrophe : the members' votes.

Les démonstratifs

  • this (singulier) / these (pluriel) : ce qui est proche, dans l'espace, le temps ou la pensée de celui qui parle : This novel is fascinating. These days…
  • that (singulier) / those (pluriel) : ce qui est éloigné ou passé : In those days, the sun never set on the Empire. That was a long time ago.

chapitres.a_retenir:
• The London Declaration (1949) created the modern Commonwealth of "free and equal" members; India and Pakistan became independent in 1947, Ghana in 1957.
  • Today: 56 member states; King Charles III is Head of the Commonwealth and head of state of 15 realms; the Commonwealth Games were first held in 1930.
  • Voices: Chinua Achebe (Things Fall Apart, 1958), Salman Rushdie, Arundhati Roy, Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie; the Windrush generation (from 1948) and Windrush Day (22 June).
  • Obligation : must, have to ; interdiction : mustn't ; absence d'obligation : don't have to ; capacité : can, be able to (aux autres temps : had to, will be able to).
  • wish + prétérit (regret sur le présent) ; wish + pluperfect (regret sur le passé).
  • Tags : auxiliaire + pronom, polarité inversée (isn't it?, do you?, didn't he?) ; réponses courtes : Yes, I have. / No, she doesn't.
  • Groupe nominal : le nom principal à la fin (a member state) ; this / these (proche), that / those (éloigné).
